feedback: If two pieces share a block, that region is being counted twice and the total will be too large — shade the two parts and assign the shared region to exactly one piece, then recount.
If an unlabelled edge was taken as a whole-figure measurement, mark the full length and subtract the known part to find the missing piece before calculating any volume.
If each part's volume is right but the sum is wrong or a piece is dropped, list every part-volume in a column and add carefully — the decomposition method itself is sound.
If a re-split gives a different total, revisit it: non-overlapping splits of the same solid must agree, so there is an overlap, omission or arithmetic slip to find.
activities.intendedInsight: Volume is additive: a composite solid can be decomposed into non-overlapping cuboids, each cuboid's volume found by l × w × h, and the parts summed — and any valid non-overlapping split rebuilds the same total.
learnerActions: Meet a step-shaped or L-shaped block with most edge lengths labelled and one or two left to deduce.
Draw a cut line to split the solid into two (or more) cuboids, then separate the pieces into an exploded view so you can see each one whole.
Check that your pieces do not overlap — no cube belongs to two pieces and none of the solid is left out.

Find any missing edge from the labelled measurements (for example, subtract the known part from the overall length, add parts to get an overall length, or use a matching parallel edge), then write down each cuboid's l, w and h.
Compute each cuboid's volume with V = l × w × h, keeping consistent cubic units (cm³ here), and add them for the total.
Re-split the same block a different valid way and confirm you get the same total.
activities.title: Pull the step-solid apart (exploded decomposition)

feedback: If pieces overlap on your diagram, you will double-count the shared region — redraw the splits so each region belongs to exactly one piece.
If a volume looks too small or too large, check whether an unlabelled edge was mistaken for a whole-figure length.
Confirm no region of the shape is left uncovered by your pieces.
activities.intendedInsight: A composite solid's volume can be computed by splitting its diagram into non-overlapping rectangular prisms, deducing missing dimensions from the whole, and summing the parts.
learnerActions: On a labelled L-shape diagram, draw split lines to divide it into non-overlapping cuboids.
Deduce each unlabelled dimension from the labelled ones (for example, by subtracting a known part from the overall measurement, adding parts, or matching an equal parallel edge), and write it in.
Compute each part's volume with l × w × h and add for the total, keeping consistent cubic units (cm³).
Try a second valid set of split lines and check the total is unchanged.
activities.title: Decompose on a diagram with dimension deduction

feedback: Check your split against the real object — do the pieces account for the whole structure without overlapping?
If the answer seems implausible, re-examine the missing-dimension deduction, the unit consistency and the final sum.
activities.intendedInsight: The additive-volume method applies to practical problems where a real object is modelled as a composite of rectangular prisms.
learnerActions: Read a real-world situation (e.g. a step-shaped concrete structure or an L-shaped container) with a labelled solid.
Decide how to split it into non-overlapping cuboids and deduce any missing dimension.
Calculate each part's volume and add for the total, giving the answer in consistent cubic units matching the labelled measurements (e.g. cm³ or m³).
State whether the total makes sense, and which part contributes the largest volume.
activities.title: Real-world composite volume problem

feedback: A total that is too large usually signals a double-counted overlap region.
A single wrong part-volume usually signals an edge taken as a whole-figure measurement instead of being deduced.
Recognising the right answer checks and reinforces the idea, but it does not by itself require building a decomposition; carry out at least one full split-and-sum yourself.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising the specific error patterns — double-counting a shared region and mis-deducing a hidden dimension — supports more reliable use of the method; selecting a correct answer is not the same as producing a decomposition.
learnerActions: Work through short items that ask you to split an L-solid, find a missing length, and compute the total.
For each item, examine the answer choices and identify which come from double-counting an overlap and which from leaving a dimension un-deduced.
Explain, in one sentence, why your chosen split avoids counting any cube twice.
Construct at least one full split-and-sum yourself so you produce the method rather than only selecting an answer.
activities.title: Spot the overlap and the missing dimension (practice items)
